questions.stem: What does a single node of a **singly** linked list contain?

options.text: A payload and a reference to the next node
A payload, a reference to the next node and a reference to the previous node
A payload and its integer index within the list
A payload and a reference to the head of the list

questions.explanation: A singly linked node stores its payload plus exactly one link, to its successor; the final node's link is null. The absence of a backward link is precisely what makes traversal one-directional and what makes deleting a node awkward when you hold only a reference to that node.

distractorRationale.b: That is a doubly linked node, which pays an extra pointer per node for bidirectional traversal
distractorRationale.c: Nodes carry no index — positions are implicit in the chain, which is why indexing costs $O(n)$
distractorRationale.d: A link to the head would make every node a circular reference to the front and would not permit traversal at all

questions.stem: What is the worst-case time complexity of retrieving the $k$-th element of a singly linked list of $n$ elements?

options.text: $O(\log n)$
$O(k \log n)$

questions.explanation: Nodes are separately allocated, so there is no arithmetic relationship between a position and an address. Reaching position $k$ means following $k$ links from the head, and in the worst case $k = n - 1$, giving $O(n)$. This loss of random access is the price paid for cheap structural modification, and it is also why binary search cannot be run on a linked list.

distractorRationale.a: $O(1)$ indexing requires contiguous fixed-width storage, which a linked list does not have
distractorRationale.b: Bisection needs random access to the midpoint, which is unavailable here
distractorRationale.d: There is no logarithmic factor; the traversal is a single linear walk

questions.stem: A new node `q` is to be inserted immediately after an existing node `p` in a singly linked list. Which sequence of assignments is correct?

options.text: `q.next = p.next` then `p.next = q`
`p.next = q` then `q.next = p.next`
`p.next = q` then `q.next = p`
`q.next = p` then `p.next = q.next`

questions.explanation: The tail of the list beyond `p` is reachable only through `p.next`, so that reference must be copied into `q.next` *before* `p.next` is overwritten. Sequence a preserves it; the general rule for all pointer surgery is to establish the new node's outgoing links first, then redirect the incoming link last.

distractorRationale.b: Overwrites `p.next` first, so the subsequent read of `p.next` already yields `q` — `q.next = q` creates a self-loop and the rest of the list is leaked
distractorRationale.c: Makes `q` point back at `p`, producing a two-node cycle and detaching the remainder of the list
distractorRationale.d: Points `q` backwards at `p` and then sets `p.next = p`, corrupting the list entirely

questions.stem: You hold a reference to a node `x` in the middle of a **singly** linked list, but not to the head. What is the cost of removing `x` from the list?

options.text: $O(1)$ — just set `x.next` to null
$O(n)$ — the predecessor of `x` must be found by traversing from the head
$O(\log n)$ — bisect the list to find the predecessor
Impossible without the head reference

questions.explanation: Removing `x` requires redirecting its predecessor's link past it, and a singly linked node offers no way to reach its predecessor, so it must be located by a linear scan from the head. In a **doubly** linked list the same removal is $O(1)$, because `x.prev` is available — this is exactly why LRU caches and intrusive kernel lists use doubly linked nodes.

distractorRationale.a: Nulling `x.next` truncates the list after `x` and leaves `x` itself still linked in
distractorRationale.c: Bisection requires random access, which a linked list does not provide
distractorRationale.d: It is possible: the copy-successor-then-delete-successor trick even achieves $O(1)$, though it fails when `x` is the tail and invalidates any external reference to the successor node

questions.stem: Inserting at the head is $O(1)$ for a singly linked list but $\Theta(n)$ for an array holding $n$ elements.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: True. Head insertion in a linked list allocates a node, sets its `next` to the current head and updates the head reference — a constant number of operations independent of $n$. In an array, order is encoded as position, so all $n$ existing elements must shift one slot right. This asymmetry is the strongest argument for a linked list, and it holds for deletion at the head as well.

questions.stem: A **doubly** linked list holds 1000 nodes on a platform where every reference occupies 8 bytes. How many bytes are consumed by link fields alone? Give a number only.
questions.explanation: Each doubly linked node carries two references, `next` and `prev`, so the link overhead per node is $2 \times 8 = 16$ bytes, giving $1000 \times 16 = 16000$ bytes in total. If the payload were a single 4-byte integer, the structure would spend four times as much memory on bookkeeping as on data — before allocator headers and alignment padding are even counted.

questions.stem: The iterative reversal of a singly linked list uses three references. In the loop body `nxt = cur.next; cur.next = prev; prev = cur; cur = nxt`, why must `nxt = cur.next` come first?

options.text: Because `cur.next` is about to be overwritten, and without a saved copy the remainder of the list becomes unreachable
Because `prev` must be initialised before the loop begins
Because reversal would otherwise take $O(n^2)$ time
Because `cur.next` must be set to null before reassignment

questions.explanation: The only reference to the unprocessed tail is `cur.next`. The next statement redirects that field backwards to `prev`, so if the value has not been captured in `nxt` first, every node after `cur` is orphaned and the list is truncated after one pass. The reversal visits each node once and performs a constant number of assignments per node, so it is $\Theta(n)$ time and $\Theta(1)$ extra space.

distractorRationale.b: `prev` is initialised to null before the loop, which is true but has nothing to do with the ordering inside the body
distractorRationale.c: Ordering the statements wrongly produces an incorrect result, not a slower one
distractorRationale.d: No nulling is required; the old value of `cur.next` is needed, which is why it is saved rather than cleared

questions.stem: An LRU cache must support lookup by key, promotion of an entry to most-recently-used, and eviction of the least-recently-used entry, all in $O(1)$ expected time. Which structure achieves this?

options.text: A dynamic array of entries ordered by recency
A hash table mapping keys to nodes of a doubly linked list holding the recency order
A singly linked list in recency order, scanned on each lookup
A binary search tree keyed on last-access timestamp

questions.explanation: The hash table gives expected $O(1)$ lookup from key to node. Because the node is doubly linked, unlinking it from its current position and relinking it at the front is $O(1)$ — no predecessor search is needed. Eviction removes the tail node, also $O(1)$ via the `prev` link. Neither structure alone suffices: the hash table has no order and the list has no fast lookup.

distractorRationale.a: Promotion in an array requires shifting elements, which is $\Theta(n)$
distractorRationale.c: Both the lookup and the predecessor search for unlinking are $\Theta(n)$
distractorRationale.d: A BST gives $O(\log n)$ rather than $O(1)$, and every access would additionally require a delete and reinsert to update the key
